Dataset title: Quarterly Survey of Public Pensions (QSPP)
Description: The Quarterly Summary of Public Pensions is a quarterly panel survey that provides national summary data on the revenues, expenditures, and composition of assets of the largest defined benefit public employee pension systems for state and local governments. Data are collected on the financial holdings and activities of the largest public-employee pension systems. The financial holdings data show assets in various types of securities such as stocks, bonds, federal notes, and mortgages. Revenue data consist of earnings, as well as contributions from governments and employees. Expenditure data consist primarily of payments to beneficiaries and withdrawals.

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.
prompts.assessment:
# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

For each category, concisely list the evidence and supporting sources that would support each risk level. Then indicate which risk level you find most appropriate and why.

Conclude with a simple summary of risk levels:
Historical Data Availability: <level>
Future Data Availability: <level>
Data Quality: <level>
Statutory Context: <level>
Staffing and Funding: <level>
Policy: <level>

-----------------------------------------------------------------------

DEPARTMENT OF COMMERCE

Census Bureau


Agency Information Collection Activities; Submission to the 
Office of Management and Budget (OMB) for Review and Approval; Comment 
Request; Quarterly Survey of Public Pensions

    The Department of Commerce will submit the following information 
collection request to the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) for 
review and clearance in accordance with the Paperwork Reduction Act of 
1995, on or after the date of publication of this notice. We invite the 
general public and other Federal agencies to comment on proposed, and 
continuing information collections, which helps us assess the impact of 
our information collection requirements and minimize the public's 
reporting burden. Public comments were previously requested via the 
Federal Register on June 6, 2024, during a 60-day comment period. This 
notice allows for an additional 30 days for public comments.
    Agency: U.S. Census Bureau, Commerce.
    Title: Quarterly Survey of Public Pensions.
    OMB Control Number: 0607-0143.
    Form Number(s): F-10.
    Type of Request: Regular submission, Request for an Extension, 
without Change, of a Currently Approved Collection.
    Number of Respondents: 100.
    Average Hours per Response: 45 minutes.
    Burden Hours: 300.
    Needs and Uses: The Quarterly Survey of Public Pensions provides a 
rich source of data on public retirement systems administered by state 
and local governments in the United States. Over 4.6 trillion dollars 
in public pension assets in the financial markets are controlled by a 
small number of large retirement systems. The frame for the 2012 Census 
of Governments identified 3,992 public retirement systems administered 
by state and local governments. The 100 largest systems, as measured by 
the system assets,

[[Page 79514]]

account for about 87.2 percent of the total assets of all systems, 
based on the 2012 Census of Governments. The Quarterly Survey of Public 
Pensions is used to collect data on the revenues, expenditures, and 
composition of assets of the 100 largest defined benefit public 
employee pension systems for state and local governments. The panel 
will be updated in 2025 based on the results of the 2022 Census of 
Governments.
    Currently, we are requesting approval to conduct the 2025, 2026 and 
2027 Quarterly Survey of Public Pensions. We are requesting no changes 
to the currently approved information collection form. The Quarterly 
Survey of Public Pensions enables policy makers and economists to focus 
on the asset base of public employee retirement systems while balancing 
respondent burden and data quality and providing a timelier subset of 
the data published in the Annual Survey of Public Pensions.
    This survey was initiated in 1968 at the request of both the 
Council of Economic Advisers and the Federal Reserve Board. The most 
important information this survey provides is the quarterly change in 
composition of the securities holdings of the defined benefit public 
employee retirement systems component of the economy. The Federal 
Reserve Board uses these data to track the public sector portion of the 
Flow of Funds Accounts. Additionally, the data are used by a variety of 
government officials, academics, students, and non-profit organizations 
to analyze trends in public employee retirement and the impact of 
retirement obligations on the fiscal well-being of state and local 
governments.
    The survey provides a focus on the asset composition of the largest 
systems. These data are already produced for existing internal and 
external needs, and most closely align with the needs of the Federal 
Reserve Board. Additionally, the related Annual Survey of Public 
Pensions (0607-0585) will continue to provide a robust collection of 
revenue and benefit data on a fiscal year basis. These data items are 
in demand on an annual basis and are already created for internal and 
external purposes by most systems as they are required items in 
Comprehensive Annual Financial Reports (CAFRs).
    Summary tables of the information collected are released quarterly 
on the internet. Documentation and explanatory materials are also 
available on the internet site here: https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/qspp.html.
    Frequency: Quarterly.
    Respondent's Obligation: Voluntary.
    Legal Authority: Title 13, U.S.C., Section and 182.
    This information collection request may be viewed at 
www.reginfo.gov. Follow the instructions to view the Department of 
Commerce collections currently under review by OMB.
    Written comments and recommendations for the proposed information 
collection should be submitted within 30 days of the publication of 
this notice on the following website www.reginfo.gov/public/do/PRAMain. 
Find this particular information collection by selecting ``Currently 
under 30-day Review--Open for Public Comments'' or by using the search 
function and entering either the title of the collection or the OMB 
Control Number 0607-0143.

Sheleen Dumas,
Department PRA Clearance Officer, Office of the Under Secretary for 
Economic Affairs, Commerce Department.

#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: Quarterly Survey of Public Pensions (QSPP)
Description: The Quarterly Summary of Public Pensions is a quarterly panel survey that provides national summary data on the revenues, expenditures, and composition of assets of the largest defined benefit public employee pension systems for state and local governments. Data are collected on the financial holdings and activities of the largest public-employee pension systems. The financial holdings data show assets in various types of securities such as stocks, bonds, federal notes, and mortgages. Revenue data consist of earnings, as well as contributions from governments and employees. Expenditure data consist primarily of payments to beneficiaries and withdrawals.

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.

# Research report: Quarterly Survey of Public Pensions (QSPP)

**Research checked:** October 9, 2026  
**Publisher:** U.S. Census Bureau, U.S. Department of Commerce  
**Official program page:** [Quarterly Survey of Public Pensions](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/qspp.html)

## Executive assessment

Your dataset identification is correct, and your description closely matches the Census Bureau’s own description. However, several qualifications are important:

- **The current official program title is “Quarterly Survey of Public Pensions.”** “Quarterly Summary of Public Pensions” also appears in Census documentation; retain it as an alternative title for discovery.
- **This is a panel of the largest state and local defined-benefit pension systems—not a census of every public pension system and not a survey of individual retirees.**
- **Its national summaries describe the covered panel.** They should not automatically be treated as totals for all U.S. public pensions.
- **Documentation and publication formats have changed over time.** In particular, the older description of releases as “three summary tables” does not match the file organization after the first quarter of 2019.
- **Historical comparisons require substantial care:** panel membership, investment classifications, imputation, mergers, and publication structures have changed.
- **Some official explanatory text is outdated or internally inconsistent.** Preserve the documentation alongside the data rather than assuming that a current webpage accurately describes every historical release.

**Overall:** QSPP is a valuable, long-running source for monitoring the financial holdings and activities of major public pension systems and supporting federal economic accounts. It is not, by itself, a measure of pension solvency, unfunded liabilities, individual retirement security, or the financial condition of every state and locality.

---

## 1. Dataset identity and verified description

### Recommended catalog description

> The Quarterly Survey of Public Pensions (QSPP), published by the U.S. Census Bureau, collects quarterly financial information from a panel of the largest state- and locally administered defined-benefit public employee pension systems. The program provides national panel summaries of pension financial holdings and activities, historically including revenues, expenditures, and asset composition. Collection began in 1968. The current program documentation describes a 100-system panel selected by total cash and security holdings, using the Census of Governments as its sampling-frame source. Coverage, classifications, questionnaires, and published products vary over time.

This preserves the substance of your description while avoiding two potential misunderstandings: that it covers all public pensions, and that every historical financial variable remains available in every current product.

### Core metadata

| Attribute | Finding |
|---|---|
| Preferred title | Quarterly Survey of Public Pensions |
| Acronym | QSPP |
| Alternative title | Quarterly Summary of Public Pensions |
| Earlier title | Survey of the Finances of Public Employee Retirement Systems; historical questionnaire labeled “Quarterly Survey of the Finances of Public Employee Retirement Systems” |
| Publisher and sponsor | U.S. Census Bureau |
| Parent department | U.S. Department of Commerce |
| Subject | Public employee pensions; state and local government finance; institutional investment |
| Collection frequency | Quarterly |
| Reference periods | Calendar quarters ending March, June, September, and December |
| Historical start | 1968 |
| Collection unit | Pension/retirement system |
| Principal public reporting level | National summaries for the covered panel |
| Current documented panel | 100 systems |
| Response obligation | Voluntary |
| Survey form | F-10 |
| OMB control number | 0607-0143 |

Sources: Census [program overview](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/qspp.html), [About page](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/qspp/about.html), [methodology](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/qspp/technical-documentation/methodology.html), and [questionnaires](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/qspp/technical-documentation/questionnaires.html).

---

## 2. Who publishes and maintains it?

The Census Bureau is both the survey’s sponsor and its statistical publisher. The Federal Reserve and Bureau of Economic Analysis are important users, **not the originating publishers**.

The operational contact is the Census public pensions team:

- **Email:** ewd.pensions@census.gov
- **Telephone:** 1-888-529-1963
- **Respondent portal:** [respond.census.gov/qspp](https://respond.census.gov/qspp)

The Bureau’s [FAQ](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/qspp/about/faq.html) identifies this team as the contact for correcting government names, revising submitted data, and verifying submissions. The current [contact page](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/qspp/about/contactus.html) also distinguishes general portal-access help from program-specific assistance.

### Funding and institutional position

The FAQ describes QSPP as part of the Census Bureau’s **Recurring Programs Area**, funded through money appropriated by Congress.

The 2024 information-collection record reports an estimated annual federal cost of **$449,000**. This is a dated administrative estimate—not a verified current budget or a separately enacted QSPP appropriation. The record is available through [Reginfo.gov](https://www.reginfo.gov/public/do/PRAViewICR?ref_nbr=202409-0607-003); its searchable [OMB.report mirror](https://omb.report/icr/202409-0607-003) provides the same administrative context.

---

## 3. Legal authority, mandate, and administrative oversight

### Statutory authority

Census identifies **13 U.S.C. §§ 161 and 182** as the survey’s authority.

- **Section 161** requires a census of governments for 1957 and every fifth year thereafter, including government receipts, expenditures, indebtedness, employees, and tax information.
- **Section 182** authorizes the Secretary to conduct surveys needed to supply annual and other interim current data on subjects covered by Title 13 censuses.

An important distinction: these provisions establish the government-statistics framework and authorize interim surveys. **They do not specifically name QSPP or require pension systems to answer this quarterly questionnaire.** Participation is voluntary.

Legal texts: [13 U.S.C. § 161](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/13/161) and [13 U.S.C. § 182](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/13/182).

### Paperwork Reduction Act / OMB clearance

The survey operates under:

- **OMB control number:** 0607-0143
- **Form:** F-10
- **2024 renewal:** extension without change
- **Approval date reported in the clearance record:** December 4, 2024
- **Expiration date:** December 31, 2027
- **Estimated respondents:** 100
- **Estimated annual responses:** 400
- **Average reporting time:** 45 minutes per quarterly response
- **Estimated annual respondent burden:** 300 hours

The [June 6, 2024 Federal Register notice](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2024/06/06/2024-12453/agency-information-collection-activities-submission-to-the-office-of-management-and-budget-omb-for) states that responses are voluntary. Its reported **$0 annual cost to the public excludes the value of respondents’ time**; it refers to additional non-time expenses associated with reporting.

### Confidentiality: a notable exception

The [F-10 questionnaire](https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/qspp/technical-documentation/questionnaires/f10.pdf) states that the data are subject to **13 U.S.C. § 9(b)**, which exempts information customarily provided in public records from the usual Census confidentiality rules.

This is important for librarians: do not simply copy the confidentiality description used for Census household or business surveys into a QSPP record.

At the same time, this exception **does not establish that every submitted record or internal processing file is available as a public download**. Public-record status, public dissemination, and access to internal Census files are separate questions.

---

## 4. Population, coverage, and representativeness

### Included systems

Census specifies two eligibility criteria:

1. The retirement system is sponsored by a recognized state or local government unit.
2. Its membership consists of public employees compensated with public funds.

The survey covers **defined-benefit plans**.

### Excluded from the stated scope

- Defined-contribution plans.
- Post-employment healthcare plans.
- Private-sector pensions.
- Federal employee retirement systems.
- Individual participant or beneficiary records.

### How the panel is selected

The methodology describes selection of the largest systems by **total cash and security holdings**, using the most recent Census of Governments: Finance Component as the frame source.

This is a size-selected panel, not a conventional random sample intended to represent systems of every size. Large plans dominate the financial totals; small local systems are outside the panel.

### Coverage percentage: an official inconsistency

The current program overview and methodology say the 100 systems account for **87.2% of financial activity**, based on the **2012 Census of Governments**.

However:

- The FAQ says **87.5%**, also referring to 2012.
- Older text in the Census trend-chart application says **89.4%**, based on 2007.

**Recommended interpretation:** use 87.2% when describing the current program documentation, but identify it as a historical benchmark. It is not a verified 2026 coverage percentage, an employee-coverage percentage, or evidence that the panel represents all smaller systems without bias.

---

## 5. What information does it contain?

The historical program description divides the information into three broad groups:

| Group | Examples |
|---|---|
| Revenues | Government contributions, employee contributions, investment earnings |
| Expenditures | Benefit payments, withdrawals |
| Holdings | Cash and investments classified by security or asset type |

Historical asset categories include corporate stocks, corporate bonds, federal government securities, mortgages, and other securities. Definitions have changed, so labels should not be treated as constant across the full time series.

### Stocks versus flows

For analysis, distinguish:

- **Holdings:** amounts at the end of the quarter.
- **Revenues and expenditures:** financial activity during the quarter.

Do not sum four quarterly holdings observations to obtain annual assets. A year-end stock or an explicitly defined annual average would be appropriate, depending on the question.

### Valuation and reporting

The questionnaire instructions specify reporting corporate stocks and bonds at **market value**. They also call for assets associated with the system’s relevant accounts and reserves.

Census warns that some systems use accrual accounting for all or part of receipts and expenditures, while others mix accrual and cash reporting. Consequently, quarterly revenues minus expenditures need not reconcile directly with the change in holdings.

### Units

The Census trend application labels total cash and security holdings in **millions of dollars** and identifies the displayed series as **not seasonally adjusted**. Always verify units and adjustment status in the particular table or API extract.

### Current publication caveat

The current-release page identifies the main product as **“Cash and Security Holdings of Major Public Employee Pension Systems.”**

The download directory shows:

- Three separate table workbooks through **2019 Q1**.
- A single quarterly workbook beginning **2019 Q2**.

This is a confirmed publication-structure change. I did not audit every workbook’s internal columns; therefore, **the older revenues/expenditures description should not be taken as confirmation that all those variables remain present in the current downloadable workbook**.

---

## 6. History and changes affecting comparability

### Panel-size history

Census’s [user notes](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/qspp/technical-documentation/user-notes.html) report:

| Period | Panel size |
|---|---:|
| 1969–1973 | 100 |
| 1974–1976 | 111 |
| 1977–1979 | 106 |
| 1980–1982 | 105 |
| 1983–1984 | 102 |
| 1985–1994 | 104 |
| 1995–1999 | Panel information unavailable in the notes |
| 2000–present | 100 |

Collection began in 1968, but this panel-history list starts in 1969.

**“No panel information” for 1995–1999 does not mean “no financial data.”** The Census trend application contains holdings observations for those years.

### Significant changes

| Date or period | Documented change | Analytical consequence |
|---|---|---|
| Before March 1978 report | Federal agency securities included in other securities | Asset-category comparisons require a crosswalk |
| 1978–1981 | Receipt estimates revised following a change in nonresponse estimation | Release vintage matters |
| March 1987 onward | Federally sponsored agency securities classified as corporate bonds | Corporate-bond series has a classification break |
| 1987–1989 | Mortgage data revised to reflect reclassification to agency securities | Historical asset composition changed through revisions |
| 2002 Q2–2004 Q3 | Investment earnings adjusted to exclude imputed data | Earnings comparisons require the footnotes |
| 2004 Q4 | Government contributions revised to include other governments’ contributions | Contribution coverage changed |
| 2009 Q1 | New panel based on the 2007 Census; five systems replaced | Changes may reflect panel composition as well as financial activity |
| 2010 Q1 | Denver Public Schools Retirement System merged into Colorado PERA | Census identifies a substantial government-contribution effect |
| 2012 Q1 | Survey renamed QSPP | Preserve older title for searching |
| 2012 Q1 | Realized and unrealized gains/losses separated | Variable comparability changed |
| 2012 Q1 | Agency securities moved from corporate bonds to federal government securities | Apparent allocation shifts may be definitional |
| 2012 Q1 | Private equity, venture capital, leveraged buyouts moved from other securities to corporate stocks | “Corporate stocks” is not simply listed equities |
| 2013 Q2 | Imputation changed to group similar systems | Processing-method break |
| 2019 | New questionnaire era; workbook organization changes after Q1 | Schema and series mapping require verification |

Sources: [methodology](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/qspp/technical-documentation/methodology.html), [user notes](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/qspp/technical-documentation/user-notes.html), [trend application](https://www.census.gov/econ_timeseries/?programCode=QPR), and the [download directory](https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/qspp/tables/time-series/current-release/).

### Bridge documentation

Census supplies a [QSPP Bridge Report for the 2012-based panel](https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/qspp/technical-documentation/user-notes/QSPP_Bridge_Report_2012_Panel.docx), describing changes associated with drawing a new top-100 panel.

Preserve this document. **Do not infer the implementation quarter solely from “2012” in its filename:** that refers to the benchmark census underlying the panel.

---

## 7. Collection, processing, revisions, and quality

### Collection

Collection starts at the beginning of the following calendar quarter and continues for approximately three months. Respondents now have an electronic reporting portal.

The usual publication lag is approximately **three months after quarter-end**, although this is not a guarantee for every release.

### Editing

Census describes checks for:

- Logical consistency between related items.
- Unusual changes relative to the prior quarter.
- Values outside acceptable tolerances.
- Cases requiring analyst review or respondent follow-up.

### Imputation

Missing or invalid answers may be replaced by estimated values. Both item nonresponse and full-system nonresponse can be imputed.

Since 2013 Q2, the documented methods include:

- Mean growth rates.
- Median growth rates.
- Direct substitution.

These methods use groupings of similar systems. Published totals therefore are not necessarily composed entirely of directly reported amounts.

### Revisions

Revisions can result from:

- Corrected respondent submissions.
- Late reports replacing imputations or estimates.

Census documents revision markers such as **“R”** and applicable figure labels. A preservation or reproducibility project should retain both the values and their revision annotations.

### Response rates: current numbers contradict older boilerplate

The methodology page says usable responses are received from “at least 80 percent” of systems. Its own newer response table, however, reports:

| Quarter | Unit response rate | Asset-weighted total quantity response rate |
|---|---:|---:|
| 2024 Q1 | 96% | 97.48% |
| 2025 Q1 | 97% | 98.24% |
| 2025 Q4 | 83% | 87.66% |
| 2026 Q1 | 76% | 82.10% |

Thus, **the “at least 80%” statement should not be treated as universally current**.

The total quantity response rate weights systems by their assets; it is not the same as the share of all U.S. pension assets covered by the panel. The table I reviewed did not yet provide 2026 Q2 response rates.

### Error risks

Census identifies classification, response, processing, interpretation, coding, and coverage errors.

For users, the principal risks include:

- Imputed or late-reported observations.
- Changes in panel composition.
- Inconsistent accounting bases.
- Category redefinitions.
- Market-value fluctuations.
- Mistaking large-system results for the entire public-pension universe.

**Absence of a conventional sampling-error estimate is not absence of uncertainty.**

---

## 8. Access, formats, API, and latest verified release

### Latest release located

The Census current-release page identified **2026 Q2** as the latest release during this research.

- [Current-release page](https://www.census.gov/data/tables/time-series/econ/qspp/current-release.html)
- [2026 Q2 workbook](https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/qspp/tables/time-series/current-release/QSPP_2026Q2.xlsx)

The file directory showed a last-modified timestamp of September 24, 2026. Treat file modification time and official publication time as distinct metadata.

### Access routes

| Resource | Purpose |
|---|---|
| [Program homepage](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/qspp.html) | Official identity and navigation |
| [Quarterly workbook directory](https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/qspp/tables/time-series/current-release/) | Direct downloads, including earlier releases |
| [Trend-chart application](https://www.census.gov/econ_timeseries/?programCode=QPR) | Historical time-series access |
| [Technical documentation](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/qspp/technical-documentation.html) | Methodology, notes, forms, layouts |
| [Unit-ID file layout page](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/qspp/technical-documentation/file-layouts.html) | Interpreting panel identifiers |
| [Census API dataset](https://api.census.gov/data/timeseries/eits/qpr.html) | Programmatic national-series access |

Confirmed formats include **XLSX workbooks**, **PDF questionnaires**, **fixed-width text unit-ID files**, and a **DOCX bridge report**.

Generic Census page text mentions CSV and PDF table downloads, but that does not prove that every QSPP release is available in every such format.

### API

A dedicated endpoint exists:

```text
https://api.census.gov/data/timeseries/eits/qpr
```

Documentation:

- [Variables](https://api.census.gov/data/timeseries/eits/qpr/variables.json)
- [Examples](https://api.census.gov/data/timeseries/eits/qpr/examples.html)

Important fields include `data_type_code`, `category_code`, `cell_value`, `seasonally_adj`, time-slot fields, and `error_data`.

The reviewed examples page states that **all data queries now require an API key**. A documented example, with your key substituted, is:

```text
https://api.census.gov/data/timeseries/eits/qpr?get=data_type_code,time_slot_id,seasonally_adj,category_code,cell_value,error_data&time=2012&key=YOUR_KEY
```

The metadata endpoint is accessible, but I did not execute a keyed data query or establish complete variable coverage for every period.

### Historical-series warning

The trend application displays a **“Pre 2019”** holdings series that has observations through 2019 Q1 and `NA` thereafter. Do not interpret those later `NA` values as missing survey collection. They signal a need to select and map the appropriate series.

### Unit IDs are not financial microdata

The current-release documentation describes the unit-ID file as the names of the 100 panel systems, in fixed-width format without delimiters.

**A panel membership list does not establish that public system-by-system quarterly financial observations are available.** This research verified public aggregate products and identifiers, not a comprehensive public financial microdata panel.

---

## 9. Typical users and public benefits

### Documented users

Census identifies:

- **Federal Reserve Board:** public-pension inputs to the Flow of Funds Accounts, now commonly associated with the Financial Accounts of the United States.
- **Bureau of Economic Analysis:** updates to government-sector national income and product accounts.
- **Investment bankers and analysts:** monitoring public pension investment patterns.
- **Economists and public-policy specialists:** economic models and government-finance analysis.

The information-collection record additionally identifies government officials, academics, students, and nonprofit organizations.

### Benefits to the public

1. **Timelier economic information.** Quarterly reporting provides a more current view than annual finance surveys.
2. **Public financial transparency.** It documents the collective financial activity of major pension systems responsible for public workers’ retirement benefits.
3. **Better national economic accounts.** Federal statistical agencies use it to help describe financial holdings and economic activity.
4. **Historical evidence.** The long series supports research on market shocks, recoveries, investment allocation, and institutional change.
5. **Lower research costs.** Standardized national summaries reduce the need to assemble comparable information independently from many systems.
6. **A common evidentiary base.** Journalists, workers, taxpayers, policymakers, and advocates can debate pension finance using an identifiable official source.

The first three uses are explicitly supported by Census documentation; the latter benefits are reasonable implications of the dataset’s public availability and historical scope.

### Appropriate policy uses—and limits

Useful questions include:

- How have major systems’ aggregate holdings changed?
- How has the reported asset mix evolved?
- What happened during market downturns?
- How much of an apparent change may reflect a classification or panel break?

QSPP alone cannot establish:

- A plan’s funded ratio or unfunded actuarial liability.
- Whether government contributions satisfy actuarial requirements.
- Whether benefits should be reduced.
- Individual retirement adequacy.
- Racial, gender, or income disparities.
- Exposure to particular companies, fossil fuels, or investment managers.
- Conditions in every small local pension system.

**A quarterly asset decline is not proof of insolvency, and a rise in assets is not proof of adequate funding.**

---

## 10. Guidance for data scientists

Recommended practice:

- **Separate stocks from flows.**
- **Build a versioned classification crosswalk**, especially for agency securities and private equity.
- **Represent panel changes and mergers explicitly** in time-series models.
- **Keep nominal and inflation-adjusted values distinct.**
- **Do not interpret holdings growth as investment return.** Contributions, payments, mergers, and panel changes also affect holdings.
- **Use response-rate information in sensitivity assessments.**
- **Parse `cell_value` cautiously:** the API declares it as a string, and missing or special values require handling.
- **Do not overwrite original files when cleaning data.**
- **Match reference quarter and release vintage**, rather than joining only on calendar year.
- **Check apparent discontinuities against questionnaires and notes before treating them as economic events.**

A useful normalized schema would include:

```text
reference_quarter
release_vintage
series_code
series_label
```

## 11. Guidance for librarians and preservationists

### Preservation priority: high

Reasons include the series’ age, its use in federal accounts, its policy relevance, and the dependence of interpretation on documentation that may change or disappear.

### Preserve the full interpretive package

For each release, retain:

1. Original workbooks and other published tables.
2. Release-page snapshots.
3. Footnotes and revision markers.
4. Questionnaire in effect.
5. Methodology and response-rate tables.
6. Unit-ID files and layouts.
7. User notes and bridge reports.
8. API responses and metadata.
9. Relevant OMB clearance materials.
10. A manifest identifying missing or unverified components.

### Specific preservation risks found

- **Mutable “current-release” locations.**
- **Inconsistent filenames:** underscores, capitalization, and prefixes vary.
- **Multiple files for the same quarter**, potentially reflecting revisions or alternative copies.
- **Outdated explanatory text:** older three-table descriptions and benchmark percentages remain online.
- **Documentation split across several locations.**
- **Incomplete panel history for 1995–1999.**
- **API and publication-schema changes.**

Directory timestamps are useful provenance clues, but not reliable substitutes for release dates or revision histories.

### Recommended repository practices

- Preserve originals; add normalized CSV or Parquet derivatives.
- Generate SHA-256 checksums and retain file sizes and retrieval timestamps.
- Store both reference periods and release dates.
- Use immutable, locally versioned release packages.
- Keep panel IDs as strings to preserve leading zeros.
- Preserve DOCX bridge documentation with an accessible derivative.
- Record parser versions, scripts, and transformations.
- Check workbook totals and footnotes after extraction.
- Keep first-release and revised values separately where possible.

### Rights and citation

Published Census statistics are generally reusable federal-government material. I did not identify a dataset-specific Creative Commons license or DOI. Record the source and applicable agency reuse policy rather than inventing a license label.

Suggested citation:

> U.S. Census Bureau. *Quarterly Survey of Public Pensions*, [reference quarter], [table/workbook or API series]. [Release or revision date, if known]. Retrieved [date], [URL].

For reproducibility, add a repository version or checksum.

## 12. Related evidence to use alongside QSPP

- **Annual Survey of Public Pensions:** broader annual pension statistics and system information; coverage and timing differ.
- **Census of Governments:** benchmark information underlying the government-finance statistical framework.
- **Federal Reserve Financial Accounts:** economy-wide pension-sector accounts incorporating additional sources and estimation.
- **BEA national accounts:** related macroeconomic measures.
- **Pension annual comprehensive financial reports and actuarial valuations:** liabilities, assumptions, funded status, and contribution requirements.
- **Detailed plan investment disclosures:** issuer- or manager-specific accountability research.

Do not expect these sources to agree exactly: universes, fiscal/calendar timing, valuation, and accounting concepts differ.

## 13. Outstanding questions and research limits

The major identity, authority, historical, user, and methodological findings are well supported. Before undertaking a definitive preservation ingest or long-run analysis, resolve:

1. **Current variable inventory:** which historical revenue and expenditure fields remain in post-2019 products?
2. **Panel refresh timing:** when was the 2012-based panel implemented, and have later benchmark-based refreshes occurred?
3. **Historical panel reconstruction:** can membership for 1995–1999 be recovered?
4. **Vintage completeness:** which files are original releases versus revised replacements?
5. **System-level access:** what quarterly financial records, if any, are publicly disseminated beyond aggregates?
6. **API continuity:** how should pre- and post-2019 series be joined?
7. **Long-term custody:** what agency records schedules and archival arrangements cover source and publication files?

This research located the official documentation, download inventory, and API metadata, but **did not audit every spreadsheet, read the full bridge report, or establish a formal archival retention schedule**. Those limits matter particularly for preservation planning.

## Bottom line

**Preserve QSPP as a versioned statistical program, not just a spreadsheet collection.** Its greatest value is its timely, long historical record of major public pension systems. Its greatest analytical hazard is treating a changing large-system panel—with revised classifications and estimated observations—as a seamless census of all public pensions or a direct measure of pension solvency.

There is also an important correction to the earlier research: **Census explicitly discontinued QSPP’s revenue and expenditure collection in the 2019 redesign**, while expanding asset detail. That supports a **High Risk** data-quality rating under your rubric when assessing the full historical dataset you described.

These ratings are **rubric classifications, not numerical probabilities of disappearance**. I distinguish actual QSPP changes from broader agency pressures, and proposed budgets from enacted cuts.

## 4. Statutory Context

### Selected level: **High Risk**

| Risk level | Evidence and interpretation |
|---|---|
| **Gone** | Not applicable. |
| **High Risk** | QSPP relies on broad government-statistics authority rather than a statute explicitly requiring this named quarterly survey. Related collections offer partial substitutes. |

### Authority and practical protection

The respondent portal cites **13 U.S.C. §§ 161 and 182**:

- [Section 161](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/13/161) establishes the quinquennial Census of Governments.
- [Section 182](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/13/182) authorizes interim surveys.

Neither specifically mandates QSPP. Responses are voluntary.

The [Federal Register continuation notice](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2024-09-30/html/2024-22365.htm) documents Federal Reserve use and describes QSPP as a timelier subset of annual public-pension information. The Federal Reserve’s [March 2026 Financial Accounts source table](https://www.federalreserve.gov/releases/z1/20260319/introductory_text.htm) confirms continuing use.

**Partial substitutes:** the Annual Survey of Public Pensions, individual pension financial reports, and economic-account estimates. None is an exact substitute for standardized quarterly panel observations. Federal Reserve publications also rely on QSPP, so they should not be treated as wholly independent replacement collections.

**Why this level:** Your High Risk definition uses “and/or”: broad authorization and partial alternative collections support that classification, despite strong programmatic use. This is a **legal vulnerability rating**, not evidence of a planned cancellation.
